Astronomy & Astrophysics

UNIONS-3500 Weak Lensing: II. B-mode validation for cosmic shear

Supporting Documents
  • ✨ASTRA Inventory

Abstract¶

At Stage-III sensitivities, cosmic shear BBB modes unambiguously indicate systematic contamination and are often used to inform data selection and scale cuts for cosmological inference. We validate BBB modes for the Ultraviolet Near-Infrared Optical Northern Survey (UNIONS)-3500 using three EEE/BBB-separable statistics: pure-mode correlation functions ξ±B(θ)\xi_\pm^{\mathrm{B}}(\theta)ξ±B​(θ), Complete Orthogonal Sets of EEE/BBB-mode Integrals (COSEBIs) BnB_nBn​, and harmonic-space power spectra CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​. We perform null tests by computing probability-to-exceed (PTE) values for each statistic and comparing the minimum PTE to a threshold of 0.01, calibrated on systematics-free simulations. BBB-mode detections on an initial catalog led us to repeat these tests for different sample selections and scale ranges before settling on fiducial cuts of 0.707 in galaxy-to-PSF size ratio, 12–83 arcmin in configuration space, and 300<ℓ<1600300 < \ell < 1600300<ℓ<1600 in harmonic space. At these cuts the fiducial catalog passes with a minimum PTE of 0.019; 13% of the systematics-free simulations have a lower PTE. When using the full range of angular scales between 1 and 250 arcmin, we measure an oscillatory COSEBI BBB-mode pattern that could be explained by a repeating additive shear bias, a detector-level effect seen across multiple Stage-III surveys including CFHTLenS, which used the same MegaCam camera; scale cuts that exclude the charge-coupled device (CCD) angular scale suppress this pattern. Although the three BBB-mode statistics probe the same two-point shear field, scale cuts applied in one basis do not map exactly onto cuts in another, because their filter functions weight angular scales differently. We therefore require scale and sample selections that pass null tests across all frameworks simultaneously, an approach that applies directly to Stage-IV surveys where systematic errors dominate.

1Introduction¶

Weak gravitational lensing distorts the observed shapes of distant galaxies, encoding information about the intervening matter distribution along the line of sight Blandford et al., 1991Miralda-Escude, 1991Kaiser, 1992. First detections came in 2000 Bacon et al., 2000Kaiser et al., 2000Van Waerbeke et al., 2000Wittman et al., 2000. The scalar gravitational potential produces a shear field that is curl-free to leading order and can be decomposed into gradient-like EEE modes and curl-like BBB modes; under the Born approximation, scalar density perturbations source only EEE-mode power Stebbins, 1996Kamionkowski et al., 1997. Higher-order effects (lens-lens coupling, source clustering, and intrinsic alignments) can produce BBB modes Hilbert et al., 2009Schneider et al., 2002Crittenden et al., 2002, but these are orders of magnitude below current sensitivity Cooray & Hu, 2002. They are likely only accessible to future ultra-high-precision measurements, potentially through cross-correlation techniques involving CMB lensing rotation reconstructions and large-scale-structure tracers Robertson et al., 2025. For galaxy shear measurements at current sensitivity, detected BBB-mode power indicates residual observational systematic effects rather than cosmological signal, though the absence of BBB modes does not rule out systematic contamination.

Stage-III cosmic shear surveys have measured the structure growth parameter S8≡σ8Ωm/0.3S_8 \equiv \sigma_8 \sqrt{\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}/0.3}S8​≡σ8​Ωm​/0.3​ at percent-level precision, with some reporting up to ∼3 σ{\sim}3\,\sigma∼3σ tension with Planck Asgari et al., 2021Abbott et al., 2022Li et al., 2023Planck Collaboration, 2020. The Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS)-Legacy Wright et al., 2025 found S8=0.815−0.021+0.016S_8 = 0.815^{+0.016}_{-0.021}S8​=0.815−0.021+0.016​ (0.73 σ\sigmaσ from Planck) and the Dark Energy Survey (DES) Y6 DES Collaboration et al., 2026 found S8=0.798−0.015+0.014S_8 = 0.798^{+0.014}_{-0.015}S8​=0.798−0.015+0.014​ (1.1 σ1.1\,\sigma1.1σ); both achieved 2%2\%2% precision on S8S_8S8​, comparable to CMB constraints from Planck alone. Stage-IV surveys will reduce statistical uncertainties further, shifting the error budget toward systematic effects; current data offer the opportunity to validate these methods before that transition.

Several methods separate EEE- and BBB-mode contributions in shear two-point statistics. Aperture mass dispersion Schneider, 1996Schneider et al., 1998 is the foundational real-space method for EEE/BBB separation. In practice, however, its evaluation requires knowledge of the shear correlation functions down to zero separation, which is unavailable on a finite observed interval and leads to EEE/BBB mixing Schneider et al., 2010Schneider et al., 2022. Complete Orthogonal Sets of EEE/BBB-mode Integrals (COSEBIs; Schneider et al. (2010), Asgari et al. (2012)) generalize this approach, compressing all EEE/BBB-separable information from ξ±(θ)\xi_\pm(\theta)ξ±​(θ) on a finite angular interval into discrete orthogonal modes. A small number of modes captures the cosmological signal; by construction, the COSEBI basis excludes the ambiguous modes that cannot be assigned pure EEE or BBB character on a finite interval. Pure-mode correlation functions ξ±E/B(θ)\xi_\pm^{\mathrm{E/B}}(\theta)ξ±E/B​(θ) Schneider et al., 2022 are an alternative real-space representation that decomposes ξ±\xi_\pmξ±​ into EEE-mode, BBB-mode, and ambiguous components through integral transforms derived from the COSEBI basis functions. Harmonic-space estimators measure CℓEEC_\ell^{EE}CℓEE​ and CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ directly but require careful treatment of mask-induced EEE/BBB mixing; catalog-based methods that evaluate spherical harmonic transforms at source positions Wolz et al., 2025 avoid the pixelization artifacts that complicate standard implementations. The HybridEB Fourier band-power estimator Becker & Rozo, 2016 constructs ℓ\ellℓ-space band-powers from linear combinations of binned ξ±\xi_\pmξ±​, projecting out ambiguous modes to minimize EEE/BBB mixing. DES Y6 adopted this estimator DES Collaboration et al., 2026, although COSEBIs are more widely used in the Stage-III literature, where they have traced systematic signatures across multiple surveys Asgari et al., 2019. These statistics represent BBB-mode power in complementary bases, and the mapping between them is not one-to-one, so contamination excluded by scale cuts in one basis may remain visible in another. Comparing across bases can expose systematics that any single framework would absorb.

Stage-III analyses have found BBB-mode contamination from a range of systematic effects. COSEBI analyses of the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope Lensing Survey (CFHTLenS), KiDS-450, and DES-SV detected significant BBB modes at 2–5 σ\sigmaσ, linked to repeating additive shear bias, PSF leakage, and photometric selection effects Asgari et al., 2019. Repeating additive shear biases can arise from detector-level defects that imprint a constant ellipticity offset on each CCD, varying across the focal plane; because this pattern is fixed in instrument coordinates, it repeats with every pointing. The bias is constant within each CCD but jumps at chip boundaries; these discontinuities carry curl, generating BBB-mode power at CCD angular scales. Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) Y3 used harmonic-space power spectra and found significant large-scale BBB modes Li et al., 2023Dalal et al., 2023. A dedicated PSF-systematics study identified PSF fourth-moment leakage as a leading additive contaminant in the affected region Zhang et al., 2023. KiDS-Legacy tested with COSEBIs, traced an initial failure to astrometric systematics, and applied conservative masking with negligible impact on S8S_8S8​ Wright et al., 2025. DES Y3 reported null detections using pseudo-CℓC_\ellCℓ​ and COSEBIs Gatti et al., 2021. However, Jefferson et al. (2025) applied the HybridEB estimator uniformly to DES-Y3 and HSC-Y3 data and found BBB-mode failures in specific tomographic bins not seen with the estimators originally used. DES Y6 subsequently adopted the HybridEB estimator and passed DES Collaboration et al., 2026. Because each estimator weights angular scales differently and deprojects ambiguous modes differently, the same data can pass one null test and fail another. The most informative validation requires consistent passage across multiple statistics.

The Ultraviolet Near-Infrared Optical Northern Survey (UNIONS; Gwyn et al. (2025)) is surveying 6250 deg² of northern sky with multi-band imaging from telescopes in Hawai’i: the Canada-France Imaging Survey (CFIS) contributes uuu- and rrr-band imaging from CFHT, Pan-STARRS contributes iii- and zzz-band data, and Subaru adds zzz-band imaging through the Wide Imaging with Subaru HSC of the Euclid Sky (WISHES) and ggg-band imaging through the Waterloo-Hawai’i Institute for Astronomy ggg-band Survey (WHIGS). Nearly all Stage-III cosmic shear survey area is in the southern sky; UNIONS provides the first deep, wide-area shape catalog in the north, with rrr-band median seeing of 0.7′′0.7^{\prime\prime}0.7′′, enabling high-quality shape measurements. Guinot et al. (2022) presented the first UNIONS weak-lensing analysis over 1700 deg² using the ShapePipe pipeline Farrens et al., 2022; the present analysis expands this to 3500 deg² with an updated catalog (Section 2).

We present BBB-mode validation tests for the first UNIONS-3500 cosmic shear cosmology analysis, using pure-mode correlation functions ξ±E/B(θ)\xi_\pm^{\mathrm{E/B}}(\theta)ξ±E/B​(θ), COSEBIs, and harmonic-space power spectra CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ to define scale cuts in both angular and multipole space within a blinded analysis framework. This paper is one of five coordinated UNIONS-3500 weak-lensing publications: catalog construction (Paper I; Hervas-Peters et al. (2026)); the present BBB-mode validation (Paper II); configuration-space cosmological constraints (Paper III; Goh et al. (2026)); harmonic-space cosmological constraints (Paper IV; Guerrini et al. (2026)); and image simulations (Paper V; Hervas-Peters et al., in prep.). We validate the fiducial scale cuts adopted for cosmological inference in Papers III and IV, both of which analyze the shear field without tomographic binning; a UNIONS tomographic analysis is now in progress. Section 2 describes the UNIONS shear catalogs, their evolution, and the simulations we use for validation. Section 3 details the three EEE/BBB-separable statistics and covariance framework. Section 4 presents the measurements and null-test results. Section 5 discusses systematic trends and methodological implications.

2Data¶

UNIONS is the largest deep weak-lensing survey of the northern sky, with rrr-band depth of r≈24.2r \approx 24.2r≈24.2 at 10 σ10\,\sigma10σ Gwyn et al., 2025. We analyze four variants of the ShapePipe v1.4 catalog, summarized in Table 1; all survey-property statistics quoted in this article are derived from that table. The initial catalog uses a loose size cut (rh,gal/rh,psf>0.5r_{\mathrm{h, gal}}/r_{\mathrm{h, psf}} > 0.5rh,gal​/rh,psf​>0.5). For the size-cut catalog, we tighten this threshold to rh,gal/rh,psf>0.707r_{\mathrm{h, gal}}/r_{\mathrm{h, psf}} > 0.707rh,gal​/rh,psf​>0.707, removing galaxies where shape measurement and leakage correction are least reliable. For the masked catalog, we retain the tightened size cut and add bright-star (r<12r < 12r<12) and faint-star (12<r<1812 < r < 1812<r<18) halo masking, reducing sky coverage by 13%. Footprint illustration shows the holes this masking cuts into the footprint, typically ∼8′{\sim}8'∼8′ across, comparable to the short side of a CCD. The relaxed-flags catalog uses the same sample selection as the size-cut catalog but relaxes the SExtractor flags criterion to include deblended objects, increasing the effective galaxy density by 26%. We introduced these refinements after blinded validation tests showed early signs of systematic contamination (Paper I). We adopt the size-cut catalog as the fiducial for Papers II, III, and IV.

For each catalog version, we produce shear measurements both with and without the object-wise PSF-leakage correction described in Paper I, which models PSF contamination via binned regression in signal-to-noise and galaxy-PSF size ratio; Guerrini et al. (2025) provide the broader PSF-leakage diagnostic framework used to assess its impact. We report results from the leakage-corrected catalogs, which are used for cosmological inference in Papers III and IV.

To validate our estimators and covariances, we use 350 lognormal simulated catalogs generated with the GLASS package Tessore et al., 2023 following the setup of Paper III. Each realization samples galaxy positions from a full-sky lognormal density field, within the survey footprint and following the fiducial redshift distribution. The galaxies carry unit weights and Gaussian intrinsic ellipticities matching the data’s σe\sigma_eσe​. The realizations thus contain sample variance (including from modes larger than the footprint), lognormal non-Gaussianity, and shape noise, but no PSF leakage or other imaging systematics. In this baseline universe, each realization is sampled on the fiducial catalog’s occupied footprint at its weight-effective galaxy count and σe\sigma_eσe​ (galaxy-density excess 0%), so the mock scatter is compared directly against the data’s own covariances (Section 3.6). The accepted paper (published universe) used the original v1.4.6.3_v2 suite, whose galaxy number density was 17% higher than that of the data and was therefore compared against covariances recomputed at the mock density; the companion cosmology papers validate their pipelines and covariances on that suite (Paper III for CosmoCov, Paper IV for NaMaster).

neffn_{\mathrm{eff}}neff​ follows Heymans et al. (2012) and σe\sigma_eσe​ is the per-component ellipticity dispersion, both from metacalibration-weighted samples. All versions share the same footprint except the masked catalog.

3.1Two-point correlation measurements¶

All BBB-mode diagnostics in this analysis use the discrete shear catalog C={(γi,wi,n^i)}i=1N\mathcal{C} = \{(\gamma_i, w_i, \hat{\mathbf{n}}_i)\}_{i=1}^NC={(γi​,wi​,n^i​)}i=1N​, comprising complex ellipticities γi\gamma_iγi​, shear weights wiw_iwi​ (Paper I), and sky positions n^i\hat{\mathbf{n}}_in^i​ for NNN source galaxies. The ellipticities γi\gamma_iγi​ are shear estimates calibrated via metacalibration Huff & Mandelbaum, 2017Sheldon & Huff, 2017: galaxy images are artificially sheared to measure the 2×22 \times 22×2 shear response matrix R\mathbf{R}R, yielding γi=R−1(ei−ci)\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i = \mathbf{R}^{-1}(\mathbf{e}_i - \mathbf{c}_i)γi​=R−1(ei​−ci​) from the observed ellipticity ei\mathbf{e}_iei​ and additive bias ci\mathbf{c}_ici​. The two-point shear correlation functions ξ±(θ)\xi_\pm(\theta)ξ±​(θ) are formed from products of tangential and cross-component ellipticities for galaxy pairs at separation θ\thetaθ. We estimate ξ±\xi_\pmξ±​ by weighting each pair by metacalibration weights and accumulating contributions in angular bins:

ξ±(θk)=∑i≠jwiwj Π(θij,θk)[γt,iγt,j±γ×,iγ×,j]∑i≠jwiwj Π(θij,θk).{\xi}_\pm(\theta_k) = \frac{\sum_{i \neq j} w_i w_j \, \Pi(\theta_{ij}, \theta_k) \left[\gamma_{\mathrm{t},i} \gamma_{\mathrm{t},j} \pm \gamma_{\times,i} \gamma_{\times,j}\right]}{\sum_{i \neq j} w_i w_j \, \Pi(\theta_{ij}, \theta_k)}.ξ±​(θk​)=∑i=j​wi​wj​Π(θij​,θk​)∑i=j​wi​wj​Π(θij​,θk​)[γt,i​γt,j​±γ×,i​γ×,j​]​.
(1)

Here γt\gamma_{\mathrm{t}}γt​ and γ×\gamma_{\times}γ×​ are the tangential and cross components of the ellipticity in the coordinate frame defined by the pair-separation vector, Π(θij,θk)\Pi(\theta_{ij}, \theta_k)Π(θij​,θk​) is the binning kernel selecting pairs with separations in bin kkk, and θij=arccos⁡(n^i⋅n^j)\theta_{ij} = \arccos(\hat{\mathbf{n}}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_j)θij​=arccos(n^i​⋅n^j​). We evaluate (1) using the tree-based correlation package TreeCorr Jarvis et al., 2004. We bin into 20 logarithmic bins over θ=1\theta = 1θ=1–250 arcmin, matching the configuration-space data-vector binning adopted in Paper III.

In harmonic space, the analogous statistics are the angular power spectra CℓEEC_\ell^{EE}CℓEE​ and CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​. We estimate these using the MASTER algorithm Hivon et al., 2002, which recovers the true CℓC_\ellCℓ​ by deconvolving the mode-coupling matrix induced by the survey geometry, as implemented in NaMaster Alonso et al., 2019. Traditional implementations operate on pixelized maps, but Wolz et al. (2025) introduced a catalog-based estimator that evaluates spherical harmonic transforms directly at source positions, avoiding pixelization artifacts. 3.2Pure EEE/BBB decomposition¶

We decompose the measured correlation functions ξ±(θ)\xi_\pm(\theta)ξ±​(θ) into pure EEE-mode, BBB-mode, and ambiguous components following Schneider et al. (2022):

ξ+(θ)=ξ+E(θ)+ξ+B(θ)+ξ+amb(θ);ξ−(θ)=ξ−E(θ)−ξ−B(θ)+ξ−amb(θ).\begin{align} \xi_+(\theta) &= \xi_+^{\mathrm{E}}(\theta) + \xi_+^{\mathrm{B}}(\theta) + \xi_+^{\mathrm{amb}}(\theta); \\ \xi_-(\theta) &= \xi_-^{\mathrm{E}}(\theta) - \xi_-^{\mathrm{B}}(\theta) + \xi_-^{\mathrm{amb}}(\theta). \end{align}ξ+​(θ)ξ−​(θ)​=ξ+E​(θ)+ξ+B​(θ)+ξ+amb​(θ);=ξ−E​(θ)−ξ−B​(θ)+ξ−amb​(θ).​​
(3)

Ambiguous modes ξ±amb(θ)\xi_\pm^{\mathrm{amb}}(\theta)ξ±amb​(θ) arise from shear patterns that cannot be assigned unique EEE- or BBB-mode origin on a finite angular interval; they take the functional forms ξ+amb(θ)=a+bθ2\xi_+^{\mathrm{amb}}(\theta) = a + b\theta^2ξ+amb​(θ)=a+bθ2 and ξ−amb(θ)=cθ−2+dθ−4\xi_-^{\mathrm{amb}}(\theta) = c\theta^{-2} + d\theta^{-4}ξ−amb​(θ)=cθ−2+dθ−4. They therefore appear on large scales in ξ+\xi_+ξ+​ and on small scales in ξ−\xi_-ξ−​, as seen in Figure 1. The pure-mode correlation functions are computed from integral transforms over the measured ξ±(θ)\xi_\pm(\theta)ξ±​(θ):

ξ+E,B(θ)=12[ξ+(θ)±ξ−(θ)±∫θθmax⁡dθ′θ′ ξ−(θ′)(4−12θ2θ′2)]−12[S+(θ)±S−(θ)];\begin{aligned} \xi_+^{\mathrm{E,B}}(\theta) &= \frac{1}{2}\left[\xi_+(\theta) \pm \xi_-(\theta) \pm \int_\theta^{\theta_{\max}} \frac{\mathrm{d}\theta'}{\theta'}\, \xi_-(\theta')\left(4-\frac{12\theta^2}{\theta'^2}\right)\right] \\ &\quad - \frac{1}{2}\left[S_+(\theta) \pm S_-(\theta)\right]; \end{aligned}ξ+E,B​(θ)​=21​[ξ+​(θ)±ξ−​(θ)±∫θθmax​​θ′dθ′​ξ−​(θ′)(4−θ′212θ2​)]−21​[S+​(θ)±S−​(θ)];​

ξ−E,B(θ)=12[ξ+(θ)±ξ−(θ)+∫θmin⁡θdθ′ θ′θ2 ξ+(θ′)(4−12θ′2θ2)]−12[V+(θ)±V−(θ)].\begin{aligned} \xi_-^{\mathrm{E,B}}(\theta) &= \frac{1}{2}\left[\xi_+(\theta) \pm \xi_-(\theta) + \int_{\theta_{\min}}^\theta \frac{\mathrm{d}\theta'\,\theta'}{\theta^2}\, \xi_+(\theta')\left(4-\frac{12\theta'^2}{\theta^2}\right)\right] \\ &\quad - \frac{1}{2}\left[V_+(\theta) \pm V_-(\theta)\right]. \end{aligned}ξ−E,B​(θ)​=21​[ξ+​(θ)±ξ−​(θ)+∫θmin​θ​θ2dθ′θ′​ξ+​(θ′)(4−θ212θ′2​)]−21​[V+​(θ)±V−​(θ)].​
(5)

Here, the +++ sign gives EEE-modes and the −-− sign gives BBB-modes. The auxiliary functions S±(θ)S_\pm(\theta)S±​(θ) and V±(θ)V_\pm(\theta)V±​(θ) enforce boundary conditions that remove ambiguous modes: ξ+amb=S+\xi_+^{\mathrm{amb}} = S_+ξ+amb​=S+​ and ξ−amb=V−\xi_-^{\mathrm{amb}} = V_-ξ−amb​=V−​ Schneider et al., 2022.

The integral transforms require finely binned ξ±\xi_\pmξ±​ over an extended angular range. We evaluate these transforms on a separate 1000-bin logarithmic grid spanning θ=0.5\theta = 0.5θ=0.5–300 arcmin, and the limits θmin⁡\theta_{\min}θmin​ and θmax⁡\theta_{\max}θmax​ in (4) and (5) are this full extent; the extended range reduces edge effects in the boundary functions S±S_\pmS±​ and V±V_\pmV±​. We apply the Schneider et al. (2022) filter kernels to this grid as a fixed linear operator, using the cosmo_numba[1] implementation Guinot & Mandelbaum, 2026 and integrating each grid cell with a Gauss–Legendre rule. We then average the resulting pure modes over each of the 20 reporting bins, weighting by pair counts. Figure 1 shows the pure EEE/BBB decomposition for the fiducial catalog.

Modes n>6n > 6n>6 are shaded; the n≤6n \leq 6n≤6 subset captures nearly all cosmological information.

COSEBIs compress ξ±(θ)\xi_\pm(\theta)ξ±​(θ) into discrete orthogonal modes EnE_nEn​ and BnB_nBn​, with clean EEE/BBB separation on finite angular intervals Schneider et al., 2010. The filter functions T±n(θ)T_{\pm n}(\theta)T±n​(θ) are constructed to satisfy boundary conditions that remove the ambiguous modes described in Section 3.2. Because the T±nT_{\pm n}T±n​ are orthonormal, different modes capture largely independent information. Each T±n(θ)T_{\pm n}(\theta)T±n​(θ) oscillates n+1n+1n+1 times across the angular interval; higher-nnn modes are therefore sensitive to increasingly oscillatory features in θ\thetaθ-space. Conversely, a feature localized in angle projects onto many modes at once, producing an oscillatory signature across the basis.

We compute the COSEBI mode amplitudes Xn∈{En,Bn}X_n \in \{E_n, B_n\}Xn​∈{En​,Bn​} over a given angular range [θmin,θmax][\theta_{\mathrm{min}}, \theta_{\mathrm{max}}][θmin​,θmax​] arcmin using logarithmic filter functions:

Xn=12∫θminθmaxdθ θ[T+n(θ)ξ+(θ)±T−n(θ)ξ−(θ)],X_n = \frac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_{\mathrm{min}}}^{\theta_{\mathrm{max}}} \mathrm{d}\theta \, \theta \left[ T_{+n}(\theta) \xi_+(\theta) \pm T_{-n}(\theta) \xi_-(\theta) \right],Xn​=21​∫θmin​θmax​​dθθ[T+n​(θ)ξ+​(θ)±T−n​(θ)ξ−​(θ)],
(6)

where the upper (lower) sign gives EnE_nEn​ (BnB_nBn​). We evaluate these integrals on the same 1000-bin grid used for the pure-mode transforms (Section 3.2). As a convergence check, we repeat the calculation on a 10 000-bin grid for the fiducial catalog and find the BnB_nBn​ amplitudes and their significance to be stable.

Figure 2 shows COSEBI BBB-mode amplitudes for the first nmax=20n_{\mathrm{max}} = 20nmax​=20 modes of the fiducial catalog. For the UNIONS data vector, the EEE-mode signal saturates by n≈5n \approx 5n≈5–6 (see Section 5), so we take n≤6n \leq 6n≤6 as the set of modes carrying most of the cosmological information, while also testing the BBB modes for all n≤20n \leq 20n≤20.

Pure-mode correlation functions (Section 3.2) can be reconstructed from the COSEBI coefficients:

ξ±X(θ)=θˉ2βθ∑n=1nmaxXn T±n(θ),\xi_\pm^{X}(\theta) = \frac{\bar{\theta}^2}{\beta_\theta} \sum_{n=1}^{n_{\mathrm{max}}} X_n \, T_{\pm n}(\theta),ξ±X​(θ)=βθ​θˉ2​n=1∑nmax​​Xn​T±n​(θ),
(7)

where θˉ=(θmin+θmax)/2\bar{\theta} = (\theta_{\mathrm{min}} + \theta_{\mathrm{max}})/2θˉ=(θmin​+θmax​)/2 and βθ=(θmax−θmin)/(θmax+θmin)\beta_\theta = (\theta_{\mathrm{max}} - \theta_{\mathrm{min}})/(\theta_{\mathrm{max}} + \theta_{\mathrm{min}})βθ​=(θmax​−θmin​)/(θmax​+θmin​). In practice, we compute the pure-mode correlation functions directly from the finely binned ξ±\xi_\pmξ±​ measurements rather than reconstructing them from the COSEBI coefficients. COSEBIs require consistent angular ranges for ξ+\xi_+ξ+​ and ξ−\xi_-ξ−​, while the pure-mode integral transforms (4) and (5) permit independent scale cuts for each.

The COSEBI modes can equivalently be computed from harmonic-space power spectra:

Xn=∑iΔℓi ℓi2π Wn(ℓi) CℓiXX,X_n = \sum_i \frac{\Delta\ell_i \, \ell_i}{2\pi} \, W_n(\ell_i) \, C_{\ell_i}^{XX},Xn​=i∑​2πΔℓi​ℓi​​Wn​(ℓi​)Cℓi​XX​,
(8)

where Wn(ℓ)W_n(\ell)Wn​(ℓ) are the harmonic-space COSEBI filter functions (Fourier duals of T±n(θ)T_{\pm n}(\theta)T±n​(θ), computed via FFT-log) and the sum runs over bandpower bins. Each Wn(ℓ)W_n(\ell)Wn​(ℓ) oscillates n+1n+1n+1 times, mirroring its real-space counterpart. A fine binning of the bandpowers is needed to resolve these oscillations, so for this transform we use 96 square-root-spaced bins, distinct from the 32 bandpowers of the direct CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ null tests (Section 3.4). The number of bins balances two requirements: too few cannot resolve the filter oscillations at high nnn, while too many lead to an unstable mode-coupling matrix deconvolution. We validated the transform on the GLASS simulations, confirming that modes n≤6n \leq 6n≤6—the range carrying nearly all cosmological EEE-mode information—agree between the two paths.

3.4Catalog-based harmonic-space power spectra¶

We estimate CℓEBC_\ell^{EB}CℓEB​ and CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ (2) directly from the discrete catalog, providing ℓ\ellℓ-dependent BBB-mode diagnostics that complement the angular-space statistics. The Wolz et al. (2025) estimator represents the survey mask as delta functions at source positions and computes the spin-2 transforms on this irregular grid using the ducc library Reinecke et al., 2023. We subtract an analytic shot-noise contribution following the implementation in Paper IV. We bin into 32 bandpowers with square-root spacing (ℓ0.5\ell^{0.5}ℓ0.5) over 8≤ℓ≤20488 \leq \ell \leq 20488≤ℓ≤2048. Figure 3 shows the measured CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ and CℓEBC_\ell^{EB}CℓEB​ for the fiducial catalog.

Validation of the BBB-mode estimators and covariances on 350 GLASS mock realizations. Top: mean BBB-mode data vector across realizations, in units of the analytic σ\sigmaσ. Shaded regions mark scales outside the fiducial cuts.

For each BBB-mode statistic, we start from the same covariance prescriptions adopted in the companion cosmology papers. In configuration space, Paper III uses CosmoCov Krause & Eifler, 2017Fang et al., 2020 to model the covariance of the shear correlation functions ξ±\xi_\pmξ±​; we compute this covariance on a 1000-bin logarithmic grid spanning θ=0.5\theta = 0.5θ=0.5–300 arcmin, using the survey properties of Paper I and the Planck 2018 fiducial cosmology Planck Collaboration, 2020. For COSEBIs and the pure-mode correlation functions, we compute the covariance as the linear transformation C=TTCξT\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{T}^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{C}_{\xi} \mathbf{T}C=TTCξ​T, where T\mathbf{T}T encodes the COSEBI filter functions or the pure-mode transforms of Section 3.2; we show the pure-mode covariance in Figure 4. In harmonic space, we use the Gaussian covariance from NaMaster’s iNKA framework for CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ and CℓEBC_\ell^{EB}CℓEB​, as Paper IV does for its BBB-mode null tests, adding non-Gaussian terms only for the EEEEEE cosmology analysis.

For all BBB-mode null tests, we retain only the Gaussian part of the covariance. In configuration space, this keeps the calculation tractable on the finely binned integration grid. This approximation underestimates the true variances because it omits connected trispectrum and super-sample covariance terms, which can also add off-diagonal structure. In Paper IV we find that adding these terms, computed with OneCovariance Reischke et al., 2025, increases the diagonal errors by about 5% at ℓ=300\ell = 300ℓ=300. In configuration space, the non-Gaussian terms contribute about 11% of the diagonal variance of ξ±\xi_\pmξ±​ within the fiducial scale cuts. The null tests are therefore conservative: a test that passes with the Gaussian-only covariance would generally pass with a more complete covariance estimate, as the simulations of Section 3.6 confirm.

Two independent checks support these covariances. Paper IV validates the harmonic-space BBB-mode covariance against Gaussian simulations (Appendix C therein), and its EEE-mode covariance against the OneCovariance code Reischke et al., 2025 and the GLASS mocks of Section 3.6. During development we also compared the analytic ξ±\xi_\pmξ±​ covariance against a jackknife estimate from the data and found ten-percent-level agreement over the fiducial angular range.

3.6Validation on simulations¶

No systematics are injected into the GLASS realizations (Section 2), so they allow us to test directly whether our estimators generate spurious BBB modes from a noise-dominated signal. In the data-matched baseline universe, these comparisons hold the mock scatter directly against the data’s own analytic covariances (Section 3.5); in the published and preprint_v2 universes, the analytic covariances are recomputed at the realizations’ galaxy density. Across the ensemble, the pure-mode decomposition, COSEBIs, and harmonic-space power spectra all recover BBB modes consistent with zero (top row of Figure 5); the mean COSEBI BnB_nBn​ deviates from zero by at most 0.14 σ\sigmaσ in any mode.

We also use the simulations to test the covariances, comparing the analytic σ\sigmaσ of each statistic with the scatter across realizations (bottom row of Figure 5). At the fiducial cuts, the median ratio of analytic to mock σ\sigmaσ over bins is 0.91–0.96 in configuration space and 1.02 in harmonic space. The agreement degrades on the large scales outside the fiducial cuts. There the analytic σ\sigmaσ is about 17% too small for the first COSEBI mode and for ξ±B\xi_\pm^{\mathrm{B}}ξ±B​ above 100′100'100′, while for CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ below ℓ≈100\ell \approx 100ℓ≈100 it is too large because EEE-to-BBB leakage is treated only approximately Nicola et al., 2021. PSF leakage already excludes these scales (Paper I), so the miscalibration does not affect our choice of scale cuts.

Data-matched baseline versus published mocks

This report renders the data-matched baseline universe, where the 350 GLASS realizations match the fiducial catalog’s footprint, weight-effective galaxy count, and σe\sigma_eσe​ (0% density excess) and are validated directly against the data covariances rather than mock-matched rebuilds. Relative to the accepted paper’s published universe (17% denser v1.4.6.3_v2 suite against mock-matched covariances), the CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ mock-to-data variance ratio over 300≤ℓ≤1600300 \le \ell \le 1600300≤ℓ≤1600 moves from 0.728 (machinery) / 0.706 (empirical) to 1.000 / 0.967; the in-cut configuration-space ⟨χ2⟩/ν\langle\chi^2\rangle/\nu⟨χ2⟩/ν tightens slightly from 1.10–1.23 to 1.05–1.19; the calibrated 5% minimum-PTE floor rises from 0.004 (0.0039) to 0.007 (0.0065); the clean-sample failure rate at the adopted threshold pthr=p_{\mathrm{thr}} = pthr​=0.01 drops from 9%9\%9% to 7%; and the global ppp-value of the fiducial catalog’s minimum PTE (0.019) moves from 14%14\%14% (50/35050/35050/350) to 13% (45/35045/35045/350). The non-Gaussian share of the fiducial ξ±\xi_\pmξ±​ diagonal variance remains 11%, and no null-test verdict or scale-cut choice changes.

3.7BBB-mode significance¶

We assess BBB-mode significance across a grid of angular scale-cut combinations. For each scale range, we test the BBB-mode data vector d⃗B\vec{d}_BdB​ against zero with χB2=d⃗BTCBB−1d⃗B\chi^2_B = \vec{d}_B^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{C}_{BB}^{-1} \vec{d}_BχB2​=dBT​CBB−1​dB​, where CBB\mathbf{C}_{BB}CBB​ is the BBB-mode covariance submatrix for the selected scale range (Section 3.5). The probability-to-exceed, PTE=P(χ2>χB2 ∣ ν)\mathrm{PTE} = P(\chi^2 > \chi^2_B \,|\, \nu)PTE=P(χ2>χB2​∣ν), is the probability that a χ2\chi^2χ2 variable with ν\nuν degrees of freedom exceeds the measured value; we set ν\nuν equal to the number of data points in the range. For the pure-mode decomposition, a scale cut selects reporting bins of the full-range decomposition, and we compute PTEs separately for ξ+B\xi_+^{\mathrm{B}}ξ+B​ and ξ−B\xi_-^{\mathrm{B}}ξ−B​, as well as a joint test ξtotB\xi_{\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{B}}ξtotB​ using the concatenated data vector and full cross-covariance. For COSEBIs, which we recompute for each angular range, we evaluate PTEs using both n≤6n \leq 6n≤6 and n≤20n \leq 20n≤20 (Section 3.3). For CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​, we apply the same framework across multipole ranges. We compute a PTE for each of the six statistics at each scale range and take the smallest PTEmin⁡\mathrm{PTE}_{\min}PTEmin​ as our test statistic. Although each PTE is expected to be uniformly distributed in the absence of BBB-modes, their minimum is skewed toward low values because the six statistics are not perfectly correlated. We therefore set the passing threshold pthrp_{\mathrm{thr}}pthr​ on the systematics-free mock realizations of Section 3.6 such that a clean sample fails 5% of the time, as would be the case for a single test at PTE =0.05=0.05=0.05. We adopt a representative single value, pthr=p_{\mathrm{thr}} = pthr​=0.01, which is conservative for nearly all scale-cut combinations; at the fiducial cuts the calibrated value is 0.007 (Figure 6). We do not apply a look-elsewhere correction for the many scale-cut combinations tested, because the BBB modes were only one of four factors that informed the scale cuts, alongside PSF leakage, modeling systematics, and the scale-cut dependence of the blinded cosmological constraints (Papers III and IV).[2]

We use the same realizations to test the χν2\chi^2_\nuχν2​ sampling distribution assumed for the PTE. The CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ PTEs are uniform, while the configuration-space PTEs skew mildly low, with ⟨χ2⟩/ν=\langle\chi^2\rangle/\nu = ⟨χ2⟩/ν=1.05–1.19. This excess matches the covariance comparison above. In configuration space the analytic σ\sigmaσ is slightly smaller than the mock scatter, which raises χ2\chi^2χ2 by the inverse square of their ratio; in harmonic space the two agree. Calibrating pthrp_{\mathrm{thr}}pthr​ on the same realizations partially absorbs this skew.

Cumulative distribution of the minimum PTE over the six statistics at the fiducial cuts, across the 350 GLASS realizations. Gray dashed lines mark the 5% quantile, which calibrates the adopted threshold pthr=p_{\mathrm{thr}} = pthr​=0.01 (solid gray lines), chosen to be conservative across nearly all scale cuts. Red lines mark the minimum PTE of the data, which 13% of realizations fall at or below. The dotted curve shows the expectation for six independent tests. The mocks generally follow this expectation because of two effects that largely cancel: correlations between the statistics raise the minimum PTE, while the slightly underestimated configuration-space covariance (Section 3.6) lowers it.

These tests were carried out within the blinded analysis framework shared with Papers III and IV. Blinding was performed on the source redshift distribution. An external coordinator generated three n(z)n(z)n(z) variants, two with random shifts, and all analysis choices were made before the true variant was revealed (Paper III). The n(z)n(z)n(z) does not enter the BBB-mode data vectors, and its effect on their covariances is negligible. We computed the covariances for each of the three variants. In configuration space they are identical, since the Gaussian BBB-mode covariance of a null signal is shape noise alone; in harmonic space they agree to better than 0.5% over the fiducial multipole range, the residual coming from EEE-to-BBB leakage from the mask. We therefore use a single variant throughout.

BBB-mode PTE values across catalog versions at fiducial and full-range scale cuts.

Fiducial scale cuts are 12–83 arcmin in configuration space and 300<ℓ<1600300 < \ell < 1600300<ℓ<1600 in harmonic space; the full range is 1–250 arcmin / 8≤ℓ≤20488 \leq \ell \leq 20488≤ℓ≤2048. A row passes the null test when its minimum PTE is at least pthr=p_{\mathrm{thr}} = pthr​=0.01; only the fiducial catalog at the adopted cuts passes.

For the fiducial catalog before scale cuts, COSEBIs fail with a 4 σ4\,\sigma4σ first mode and both pure-mode correlation functions fail, while CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ passes but shows low-level BBB-mode structure (Table 2). At the adopted scale cuts, the fiducial catalog passes with a minimum PTE of 0.019; 13% of the systematics-free realizations have a lower PTEmin⁡\mathrm{PTE}_{\min}PTEmin​ (Figure 6). We chose those cuts using the BBB-mode tests together with additional systematics checks and blinded inference-stability checks in Papers III and IV. The object-wise PSF-leakage correction (Paper I) shifts individual PTEs by at most 0.093 across all catalog versions and statistics; no pass/fail conclusion changes. We report leakage-corrected results throughout.

The low-level features that drive the full-range behavior leave different signatures in each statistic. In the pure-mode decomposition (Figure 1), ξ+B/σ\xi_+^{\mathrm{B}}/\sigmaξ+B​/σ shows a broad positive excess on the smallest angular scales that tapers toward zero by θ∼10\theta \sim 10θ∼10 arcmin, apart from a ∼3 σ{\sim}3\,\sigma∼3σ outlier in the 9–12 arcmin bin, just below the fiducial lower cut. This outlier appears in all four catalog versions (Figure 7) and coincides with a jump in the total ξ+\xi_+ξ+​, at roughly the angular size of a MegaCam CCD. The corresponding ξ−B\xi_-^{\mathrm{B}}ξ−B​ is quieter on the smallest scales but remains broadly elevated from roughly 7 arcmin to the largest scales. The COSEBI data vector (Figure 2) compresses the same structure into a smaller number of modes: on the full angular range, the first mode reaches 4 σ4\,\sigma4σ and the higher modes show coherent oscillations, whose possible origins we discuss in Section 5; after applying the fiducial angular cuts, the first-mode excess drops below 1 σ\sigmaσ and the oscillatory pattern largely disappears. In harmonic space (Figure 3), CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ shows a low-level positive offset across much of the fiducial range, with the most conspicuous outliers near ℓ≈125\ell \approx 125ℓ≈125 and 250, and above ℓ≈1600\ell \approx 1600ℓ≈1600. Even so, the fiducial range 300<ℓ<1600300 < \ell < 1600300<ℓ<1600 passes the null test, while CℓEBC_\ell^{EB}CℓEB​ remains consistent with zero, suggesting that any BBB-mode contamination is not strongly correlated with the lensing signal.

Figure 7 compares the BBB-mode measurements across catalog versions, and Table 2 summarizes the PTEs. At the fiducial cuts, ξ+B\xi_+^{\mathrm{B}}ξ+B​ and COSEBIs pass for all four versions, whereas ξ−B\xi_-^{\mathrm{B}}ξ−B​ shows a broad positive excess from roughly 7 arcmin to the largest scales in every version, driving failures in all but the fiducial catalog. The fiducial catalog passes, but at the edge of its ξ−B\xi_-^{\mathrm{B}}ξ−B​ acceptance region (Figure 10). In harmonic space (Figure 11), the initial and relaxed-flags catalogs fail across most multipole combinations, whereas the fiducial and masked catalogs show broad acceptance regions. Only the fiducial catalog passes all statistics at the adopted cuts.

At full range, all versions show low-order oscillatory structure consistent with the repeating additive pattern discussed below, driving COSEBI (n≤6n \leq 6n≤6) PTEs to 1.37 × 10⁻⁵ or below; at fiducial cuts, all versions pass, although the initial catalog retains a mild oscillatory pattern.

Figure 11 and Figure 10 map null-test performance over the full grid of scale-cut combinations. In the configuration-space maps, ξ+B\xi_+^{\mathrm{B}}ξ+B​ and COSEBI failures concentrate at small θmin⁡\theta_{\min}θmin​, below the fiducial cut. For COSEBIs, whose data vector is indexed by mode number rather than angle, the PTE heatmap translates null-test performance back into angular space.

5Discussion¶

The pure-mode correlation functions, COSEBIs, and harmonic-space power spectra presented in this paper weight angular scales and treat ambiguous modes differently, so they do not respond identically to the same contamination. When they disagree, we treat that as evidence of contamination in the sample even if each statistic is not equally sensitive to it, and require the adopted catalog and cuts to pass in all three frameworks.

At full range, all four catalogs show a COSEBI first-mode excess exceeding 4 σ4\,\sigma4σ and oscillatory structure across all twenty modes. Because COSEBIs are orthogonal over a finite angular range (Section 3.3), a feature compact in angle spreads across the mode spectrum; the full-range oscillations are qualitatively consistent with contamination at CCD angular scales (Section 4, Figure 2). In the pure-mode data vectors, ξ+B\xi_+^{\mathrm{B}}ξ+B​ shows a ∼3 σ{\sim}3\,\sigma∼3σ outlier in the 9–12 arcmin bin, at CCD scales, where the total ξ±\xi_\pmξ±​ also show noticeable breaks (Figure 1). In harmonic space, CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ has a few ≳2 σ{\gtrsim}2\,\sigma≳2σ outliers at low ℓ\ellℓ and elevated power in the highest multipole bins, without a sharp angular signature that would point unambiguously to CCD-scale contamination. MegaCam’s 40 CCDs (Footprint illustration) span 6–14 arcmin individually, and our adopted lower cut of 12 arcmin excludes most pair separations at these scales; at the adopted scale cuts, the COSEBI features are suppressed and the COSEBI tests pass for all four catalogs. Pure-mode correlation functions and CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ on the other hand pass at the adopted cuts only for the size-cut catalog and for the size-cut and masked versions, respectively. These equivocal results lead us to argue against relying on any single null test; taken together, we choose the size-cut catalog and our adopted scale cuts as the combination least affected by systematic contamination for cosmological inference in Papers III and IV.

COSEBI EnE_nEn​ (top row) and Bn/σnB_n/\sigma_nBn​/σn​ (bottom row) for the fiducial catalog, computed from configuration-space ξ±\xi_\pmξ±​ (filled circles) and harmonic-space bandpowers (open squares). Modes n>6n > 6n>6 are shaded; for n≤6n \leq 6n≤6, where the cosmological information is concentrated, we confirm consistency between the two paths on GLASS simulations.

Although the masked catalog passes in ξ+B\xi_+^{\mathrm{B}}ξ+B​, ξtotB\xi_{\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{B}}ξtotB​, harmonic space, and COSEBIs (n≤6n \leq 6n≤6), this ostensibly more conservative choice fails in ξ−B\xi_-^{\mathrm{B}}ξ−B​. Excising stellar halos introduces irregular gaps in the survey footprint (Footprint illustration), and because BBB-modes are non-local, a more complex mask geometry may increase the fraction of modes classified as ambiguous, leaving the remaining pure-mode estimates less stable; alternatively, removing regions of elevated shape noise near bright stars could increase the significance of contamination elsewhere. We cannot distinguish these explanations with the present data. Our footprints are reconstructed by binning the catalog’s per-object mask flags onto a HEALPix grid (Paper I) rather than taken directly from the underlying pixelized masks; the UNIONS tomographic analysis now in progress defines the footprint from the pixelized masks themselves, which will allow a better understanding of the impact of the masks on the data. The initial and relaxed-flags catalogs fail in ξ−B\xi_-^{\mathrm{B}}ξ−B​ and harmonic space, consistent with poorly resolved or deblended objects contributing to the contamination; the relaxed-flags catalog also shifts the total ξ+\xi_+ξ+​ systematically higher than the other versions beyond 16 arcmin (Figure 7), suggesting that admitting these objects affects the signal itself, not only the BBB-mode diagnostics.

Configuration-space and harmonic-space estimators respond differently to the same contamination. Pure-mode correlation functions are localized in angular separation, so cuts that remove CCD-scale separations directly reduce the contamination. In multipole space, a feature narrow in angle maps onto a broad range of ℓ\ellℓ, so it cannot be isolated by cutting a localized multipole range. COSEBIs apply filter functions to the two-point statistics that concentrate cosmological information into the first few modes; contamination at a characteristic angular scale spreads across the mode spectrum rather than isolating in a single mode. Pure-mode and COSEBI filters also discard ambiguous modes (Section 3.2) that cannot be uniquely classified as EEE or BBB on a finite angular interval. The harmonic-space estimator used here does not deproject ambiguous modes; it assigns all power to CℓEEC_\ell^{EE}CℓEE​ or CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​, and any residual mask-induced EEE-to-BBB leakage after mode-coupling deconvolution is absorbed into CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​.

We show directly that CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ and COSEBIs have different sensitivity to systematic features, even when computed from the same data, by transforming the harmonic-space bandpowers into COSEBIs ((8)). The CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ power spectrum passes the null test at our fiducial multipole range, yet COSEBIs computed from the same harmonic-space data fail at full angular range—because the COSEBI filter functions Wn(ℓ)W_n(\ell)Wn​(ℓ) weight the power spectrum differently, concentrating sensitivity on the scales where the contamination resides. This provides empirical support for the argument of Asgari et al. (2019) that a null test in one representation cannot validate another; Jefferson et al. (2025) reached the same conclusion across DES-Y3, KiDS-1000, and HSC-Y3, finding that tomographic bins passing pseudo-CℓC_\ellCℓ​ BBB-mode tests can fail when reanalyzed with HybridEB. The converse also holds: a BBB-mode failure in any statistic should raise concern for cosmological inference in all of them, since the underlying contamination is present in the data regardless of how it is projected.

Figure 12 compares COSEBIs computed from configuration-space ξ±\xi_\pmξ±​ and from harmonic-space bandpowers. Both EnE_nEn​ and BnB_nBn​ agree across the two computation paths for all twenty modes, with the tightest correspondence in the first six modes validated on GLASS simulations. At fiducial scale cuts, both paths yield BBB-modes consistent with zero (PTE == =0.6 harmonic, 0.78 configuration; n≤6n \leq 6n≤6). At full range, both detect the same structure (PTE == =1.62 × 10⁻⁵ and 1.37 × 10⁻⁵). This confirms that the sensitivity to systematic contamination is set by the filter functions, not by the basis in which the two-point function is measured. Throughout this analysis, we use Gaussian-only covariance, which underestimates variances for the UNIONS geometry (Section 3.5); the reported PTEs are therefore conservative.

Asgari et al. (2019) identified an oscillatory COSEBI BBB-mode pattern in multiple Stage-III surveys—CFHTLenS, KiDS-450, and DES-SV—tracing it to a repeating additive shear bias (i.e. a spatially varying ccc-term) from detector-level effects fixed in focal-plane coordinates. Its appearance across three Stage-III surveys points to a detector-level phenomenon rather than a pipeline-specific artifact, a point especially relevant for UNIONS because CFHTLenS also used MegaCam on CFHT Heymans et al., 2012Guinot et al., 2022. The dither strategy, however, differs substantially. CFHTLenS and KiDS used small dithers designed to bridge chip gaps, so the focal-plane pattern maps almost directly onto the sky. UNIONS dithers by ∼1/3{\sim}1/3∼1/3 of the MegaCam field of view Gwyn et al., 2025, larger than a single CCD, so each sky position averages the additive bias from several different CCDs across exposures. Asgari et al. (2019) note that the BBB-mode signature of a repeating additive pattern depends on the dithering strategy, pointing to DES-SV’s half-field dithers as one reason its pattern differs from the small-dither surveys. The larger UNIONS dithers may similarly attenuate the amplitude of the repeating pattern, but are unlikely to fully eliminate it: the effective pattern is the per-CCD bias convolved with the dither geometry, potentially spreading the characteristic angular scale beyond the 6–14 arcmin CCD footprint.

A repeating additive shear bias could itself be created by PSF leakage that is tied to an instrumental or observational scale. The ρ\rhoρ-statistics and ξsys\xi_{\mathrm{sys}}ξsys​ diagnostics of Paper I show a feature near the ∼10{\sim}10∼10 arcmin size of a MegaCam CCD, consistent with CCD-scale leakage. In the simulations of Asgari et al. (2019), spatially varying PSF leakage mainly raises the low COSEBI modes, while a repeating additive bias produces oscillations across modes; our full-range first-mode excess and oscillations resemble these signatures respectively. However, leakage correction does not significantly change either feature (Section 4), pointing to either a different origin for the BBB-modes or leakage beyond our second-order model from higher-order PSF moments Zhang et al., 2023.

Paper V discusses a possible pipeline-specific source arising from the improper propagation of exposure offsets within the shape measurement pipeline. In the current multi-exposure fitting procedure, objects are effectively assumed to be centered on the pixel grid of each individual exposure. However, a consistent treatment would require recentering the model using the World Coordinate System (WCS), anchored to the detection position defined at the tile level. In areas where CCDs overlap, the relative pixel offsets between exposures can induce a preferred orientation in the inferred galaxy shapes, corresponding to the vector displacements between exposure pixel grids. As a result, a coherent additive shear pattern may be imprinted across the CCD overlap regions, on angular scales between the per-CCD footprint (∼6\sim 6∼6–14 arcmin) and the UNIONS dither spacing (1/31/31/3 MegaCam FoV, or ∼19\sim 19∼19 arcmin). The observed BBB-mode contamination concentrates at θmin≲\theta_\mathrm{min} \lesssim θmin​≲12 arcmin (Figure 10), close to the per-CCD scale but below the dither offsets. Whether this mechanism is responsible for the observed BBB modes remains an open question. Even so, a contamination localized near the CCD scale would be cut away in configuration space, while its Hankel transform to harmonic space would spread across multipoles, beyond any single ℓ\ellℓ cut. If a comparable additive contribution were present in the EEE modes, it would lift the harmonic-space S8S_8S8​ relative to configuration space, and could contribute to the mild offset seen between Papers III and IV. Including configuration-space scales down to 5 arcmin does move its S8S_8S8​ toward the harmonic value (Paper III). While a fraction of these effects may be absorbed by standard multiplicative bias corrections, we mitigate any remaining impact on cosmological constraints by cutting the majority of CCD scales.

An alternative to excluding contaminated scales would be to model the BBB-mode signal as a bias and subtract it from the total measurement. However, the relationship between EEE- and BBB-mode contamination depends on the physical mechanism; Asgari et al. (2019) showed that different systematics produce markedly different EEE/BBB ratios, so the BBB-mode amplitude alone does not determine the EEE-mode contamination. We therefore treat BBB-modes as a diagnostic rather than a correction: scale cuts that remove BBB-mode contamination also remove any corresponding contamination of the total signal, without assuming a model for the relationship between them.

6Conclusions¶

UNIONS-3500 weak-lensing BBB modes are consistent with zero at the adopted scale cuts across pure-mode correlation functions, COSEBIs, and harmonic-space power spectra. Without scale cuts, ξ+B\xi_+^{\mathrm{B}}ξ+B​ and the COSEBIs show significant BBB modes on small scales, whereas ξ−B\xi_-^{\mathrm{B}}ξ−B​ and CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ show a broad, low-level excess with little scale dependence; this excess is significant in ξ−B\xi_-^{\mathrm{B}}ξ−B​ on large scales and marginal at the fiducial cuts.

On the full angular range, all catalog versions show an oscillatory COSEBI BBB-mode pattern plausibly caused by a repeating additive shear bias at CCD angular scales Asgari et al., 2019. This is especially relevant for UNIONS because a similar signature also appeared in CFHTLenS, which likewise used MegaCam on CFHT Heymans et al., 2012Guinot et al., 2022. Our adopted lower cut suppresses this pattern without discarding the angular scales that carry most of the cosmological signal. By computing COSEBIs from the harmonic-space bandpowers, we confirm that the disagreement is not a matter of harmonic versus real space: CℓBBC_\ell^{BB}CℓBB​ passes where COSEBIs fail, because the COSEBI filter functions concentrate sensitivity on the contaminated scales.

Of the four catalog variants tested, only the fiducial passes in every representation. Each statistic responds differently: tightening the galaxy-size cut suppresses BBB-mode power in ξ−B\xi_-^{\mathrm{B}}ξ−B​ and harmonic space; adding stellar-halo masks causes a failure in ξ−B\xi_-^{\mathrm{B}}ξ−B​; and COSEBIs (n≤6n \leq 6n≤6) pass for all versions, even though the full-range measurements show strong low-order structure. These differences arise because the same contamination projects differently into angular, modal, and multipole representations; demanding that all three frameworks pass simultaneously places tighter constraints than any single null test. Papers III and IV adopt these fiducial cuts for cosmological inference.

Because the underlying contamination is present in the data regardless of how it is projected, a BBB-mode failure in any one framework warrants scrutiny across all of them. Rather than modeling BBB-modes as a bias to subtract, we use them as a diagnostic: scale cuts that remove BBB-mode contamination also remove any corresponding contamination of the cosmological signal, without assuming a model for the EEE/BBB ratio. Whether the same CCD-scale effects arise in Euclid and the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), with their different detector geometries and dithering strategies, remains to be seen. As surveys become systematics-limited, disagreements between BBB-mode estimators will carry as much information as their agreements; multi-framework validation will be needed to distinguish instrumental contamination, pipeline effects, and residual astrophysical signals.

Data Availability¶

A subset of the raw data underlying this article is publicly available via the Canadian Astronomical Data Centre at http://www.cadc-ccda.hia-iha.nrc-cnrc.gc.ca/en/megapipe/. The remaining raw data and all processed data are available to members of the Canadian and French communities via reasonable requests to the principal investigators of the Canada-France Imaging Survey, Alan McConnachie and Jean-Charles Cuillandre. A public release of the shear catalog will follow the acceptance of Paper I; the products of this paper are available from the authors on request.
